entries.title: Second person charged with murder after man shoved from moving Red Line train
entries.summary: <p>A second person has been charged with murder in the death of 29-year-old Kyle Bickham, who was shoved from a moving CTA Red Line train earlier this month.</p><p>Katlar Parchman, 19, faces one count of first-degree murder, two additional murder counts, one count of aggravated battery of a transit employee, and one count of mob action, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Parchman was arrested Wednesday in the 200 block of North Keeler Avenue after investigators identified her as one of the people who allegedly helped push Bickham from a moving train Sept. 7 near the 69th Street station, police said.</p><p>A fight had broken out aboard the train before three people reportedly shoved Bickham onto the electrified third rail. He was then struck by another train and pronounced dead at the scene, according to police.</p><p>The Cook County medical examiner’s office determined Bickham died of multiple injuries and ruled his death a homicide.</p><p>A 15-year-old girl was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/13/15-year-old-girl-charged-murder-man-shoved-cta-red-line-train" target="_blank" >previously charged</a> with murder, mob action and felony assault of a transit employee in connection with Bickham’s death.</p><p>She was ordered detained during her first court appearance on Sept. 12, according to the Cook County state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>Area 1 detectives continue to investigate, police said.</p>

entries.title: Man, 41, dies after shot in face in South Shore
entries.summary: <p>A 41-year-old man was fatally shot in the South Shore neighborhood Saturday evening, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man was struck in the face by gunfire along the 7500 block of South Kingston Avenue at about 6:36 p.m., police said.</p><p>He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, according to police.</p><p>Area detectives are investigating.<br></p>

entries.title: Kamilla Cardoso still believes in the Sky’s future — and coach Tyler Marsh
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — Another day, another beat down, this time at the hands of the Dream.</p><p>Despite the rough finish to the season, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> center <b>Kamilla Cardoso</b> remains confident about where the team is headed next year.</p><p>“I think we have a great squad,” she told the Sun-Times. “I think injuries messed us up a little bit, but I believe we have a great squad to make it to the playoffs and win a championship.”</p><p>Cardoso will enter the final year of her rookie contract next season. A championship is almost certainly still a ways off, but the Sky should benefit from better health and another year of development for their young core.</p><p>First, they must decide who will oversee that development.</p><p>Coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> has been on the hot seat given the team was expected to make the playoffs. But Cardoso, who has praised Marsh’s offensive system throughout the season, gave him a vote of confidence.</p><p>“I think Tyler is an amazing coach,” she said. “I think he’s doing a great job and everything that he possibly can to help us. I do think he’s the right fit and I’m really excited to see what the future holds.”</p><p>If Marsh returns for a third season, he’ll have plenty of continuity to work with. Nine of the 13 players on the roster are under contract, and the Sky will have two first-round draft picks, one from the Dream and one from the Mystics.</p><p>The key will be making sure their young talent takes another step.</p><p>Cardoso had her best season yet, averaging 14.7 points and 8.7 rebounds, but parts of her game remain raw. She still doesn’t shoot much outside the paint, and foul trouble hurts her defensively.</p><p>This offseason, Cardoso is going to play in Project B, the five-on-five touring league launching in January. Before then, she’ll spend a few weeks at home in Brazil, then return to Chicago to train before Project B begins.</p><p><b>Respectable rookies</b></p><p>Three rookies in the starting lineup offered some support for Cardoso’s optimism. With veterans managing their injuries, rookies <b>Aicha Coulibaly</b> and <b>Gabriela Jaquez </b>made the most of their starts.</p><p>Coulibaly scored 11 points in the first half, continuing to show more polish on her drives. Jaquez<b> </b>looked more like the player from her first 15 games and finished with 14 points and 2 steals.</p><p>“Just being aggressive, trying to help the team win,” Jaquez said of her performance.</p><p>But the wheels came off when the Dream turned up the pressure in the second half, and the Sky fell 106-to-81.</p><p>Turnovers and poor three-point shooting once again hurt the Sky. So did their former star, <b>Angel Reese, </b>who<b> </b>scored 23 points on 9-13 shooting.</p><p><b>Taylor troubles</b></p><p>Taylor had another rough night. She picked up three early fouls and finished with two points on 1-8 shooting.</p><p>“I think one of Sydney’s growth areas is just not getting distracted when [her] shot’s not falling,” Marsh said. “There’s other ways that she can continue to be effective.”</p><p>Taylor did show off some nifty playmaking with two highlight-reel passes in the first half, but overall the Dream’s physicality gave her trouble.</p>

entries.title: With Dream surging, Sky’s Angel Reese trade looks worse than ever
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — The last time the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> were in Atlanta in mid-July, there was at least a glimmer of hope in the trade that sent Angel Reese to the Dream for first-round picks in 2027 and 2028.</p><p>The Dream were slumping and had recently fallen as low as seventh in the standings. That meant the value of the Sky’s 2027 pick was rising, and maybe Reese wasn’t the missing piece Atlanta needed to reach the WNBA Finals after all.</p><p>With a week remaining in the regular season, that hope has vanished.</p><p>The Dream are now preparing for a championship run as top 4 team. And not only has Reese been their most consistent player, averaging 16.5 points, 12.4 rebounds and 1.8 steals, but she’s even in the conversation for her first All-WNBA selection.</p><p>She reminded the Sky of that Saturday night, leading the Dream to a 25-point rout.</p><p>Meanwhile, the Sky’s big roster revamp, headlined by the Reese trade, once again has them on the outside of the playoff picture.</p><p>A tough pill to swallow, especially since they don’t own their own 2027 pick and the one they’ll get from the Dream is likely to land late in the first round.</p><p>There is, at least, a caveat for Sky fans.</p><p>From a big picture perspective, this past offseason wasn’t really about swapping Reese for draft picks. It was swapping Reese for Rickea Jackson as the new face of the franchise. Jackson’s promising start lasted only four games before she tore her ACL.</p><p>So the final judgment on the Reese trade will have to include Jackson. Does she have a chance to become as good a player as Reese? Maybe. She’s already the better shot-creator and oozes talent and athleticism. After all, she was drafted three spots ahead of Reese in 2024, at No. 4.</p><p>But Jackson never totally proved herself during her first two years in Los Angeles, nor did she get the chance to in Chicago this season.</p><p>Reese already has, and then some.</p><p>She’s now a three-time All-Star, fresh off winning gold at the FIBA World Cup. She entered the league as a historically gifted rebounder and has quickly become one of its best defenders.</p><p>When asked to make Reese’s case for first-team All-Defensive honors, Dream coach Karl Smesko was shocked that anyone would need to hear it.</p><p>According to Smesko, all the advanced metrics point in favor of Reese. And if fancy statistics aren’t your thing, just watch her defend the pick-and-roll. At 6’3, she can both protect the rim and wreak havoc for guards, picking off their passes or slapping the ball out from under them.</p><p>“Case closed,” Smesko said.</p><p>The only question in Smesko's mind is whether she’ll be Defensive Player of the Year.</p><p>The Sky don’t have anyone in the All-Defensive conversation, much less the one for DPOY. Their team defense hasn’t been terrible this season; they rank eighth in defensive efficiency. But serious defenses in the WNBA need serious rim protection, and neither starting big, Kamilla Cardoso nor Azurá Stevens, has been physical enough around the rim.</p><p>Could Jackson help change that? She came into training camp sounding motivated to turn over a new leaf defensively, but it has never been her forte, and players don’t become elite defenders overnight.</p><p>Reese, by contrast, has been calling her shot since she was a rookie in Chicago. Defensive Player of the Year is where she has always believed she’s headed.</p><p>Sending away a star with that kind of mindset comes with consequences. Saturday night was one of them.</p>

entries.title: 1 dead after shooting in North Lawndale
entries.summary:
An unidentified person was killed in a shooting in North Lawndale Saturday afternoon, Chicago police said.

Police said the male victim was in an alley along the 3900 block of West 18th Street at about 4:34 p.m. when someone approached him in an unknown vehicle and fired shots.

The victim was struck in the face, abdomen and leg, according to police.

He was initially taken to Mount Sinai Hospital and reported in critical condition before he was later pronounced dead, police said.

Area detectives are investigating.

entries.title: Fire fall to Eastern Conference-leading Nashville
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Sam Surridge scored in the first half and Brian Schwake finished off his league-leading 12th clean sheet of the season as Nashville SC clinched a playoff spot and remained unbeaten at home with a 3-0 victory over the Chicago Fire on Saturday night.</p><p>Eastern Conference-leading Nashville (17-3-6) leads the Supporters' Shield race and is the only team in the league unbeaten at home with a 12-0-1 record.</p><p>Surridge staked Nashville to a 1-0 lead in the 33rd minute and it stood through halftime.</p><p>Cristian Espinoza added an insurance goal in the 78th minute and Hany Mukhtar scored in the 87th to set the final margin.</p><p>It was the 16th goal of the campaign for Surridge, the fourth for Espinoza and the 11th for Mukhtar as the whole front line for Nashville found the net.</p><p>Schwake, a 25-year-old first-year starter, notched one save and has surrendered only 21 goals through 26 starts.</p><p>Chris Brady saved two shots for Chicago (11-8-6), which has lost two straight following a seven-match unbeaten streak.</p><p>The Fire handed Nashville its first loss of the season with a 1-0 victory at Soldier Field on April 4. Philip Zinckernagel scored 16 seconds into that match for the lone goal — the earliest scored in Fire history.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Chicago: At Charlotte FC on Saturday.</p><p>Nashville: Hosts Toronto FC on Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Man critically wounded after being shot Saturday morning in Douglas
entries.summary: <p>A 47-year-old man was hospitalized for critical injuries early Saturday after he was shot in the Douglas neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers responded to a call of a person shot at about 3:29 a.m. along the 3600 block of South King Drive, where they found the man on the ground with a gunshot wound to the groin, police said.</p><p>Chicago Fire Department medics treated the man at the scene and took him to the University of Chicago Medical Center, according to police. He was listed in critical condition.</p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating the incident.</p>

entries.summary: <p>A 45-year-old man was critically injured in a shooting in Garfield Park early Saturday, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man had been outside along the 3900 block of West Madison Street at about 7:07 a.m. when he was shot, according to police.</p><p>The wounded man took himself to Mount Sinai, where he was listed in critical condition, police said.</p><p>No other injuries were reported. entries.title: Notre Dame has little trouble getting past Michigan State
entries.summary: <p>SOUTH BEND, Ind. — C.J. Carr threw for 234 yards and ran for a touchdown, Nolan James Jr. rushed for 121 yards and a score, and No. 3 Notre Dame took control in the second half to beat Michigan State 27-10 on Saturday night.</p><p>It was the 13th straight victory dating to last season for the Fighting Irish — all by double digits. Coach Marcus Freeman broke the Notre Dame record for consecutive double-digit victories, exceeding the 12 by Knute Rockne from 1921-22.</p><p>Micah Gilbert had eight catches for 170 yards, the most yards for a Notre Dame receiver since 2019.</p><p>Carr's streak of 12 games with a passing touchdown ended, with the Fighting Irish (3-0) scoring all three TDs on short rushes.</p><p>Notre Dame outscored Michigan State 10-0 in the second half, limiting the Spartans (2-1) to 40 yards of offense over the final two quarters. Michigan State only had one play in Notre Dame territory in the second half, and a 9-yard sack sent the Spartans back into their own territory.</p><p>“It wasn’t perfect, as everybody saw, but it was a good victory and a hard-fought victory,” Freeman said. “Those are the type of victories that you’re going to have to win and find a way to win.”</p><p>Notre Dame punished the Spartans with four quarterback sacks, six tackles for loss and two interceptions, by Luke Talich and Adon Shuler.</p><p>“We make that a staple of our defense,” linebacker Drayk Bowen said. “We want to take the ball away. We want to be at least plus-two in every game. It’s intentional work in practice ... whether it’s a punch-out or we have a chance to intercept it.”</p><p>Carr's 3-yard run early in the fourth quarter made it 27-10. James scored on a 2-yard run in the first quarter, and Aneyas Williams ran it in from 1 yard out with 4:46 left in the second.</p><p>Williams' TD made it 17-3, but the Spartans closed within 17-10 by halftime. Cam Fancher, who platooned with Alessio Milivojevic at quarterback, scored on a 15-yard scramble.</p><p>Milivojevic was 9 of 17 passing for 123 yards and the two picks.</p><p>Michigan State coach Pat Fitzgerald said Notre Dame's quick start wounded the Spartans' chances for an upset.</p><p>“We had talked to them about avoiding the first-round knockout, and obviously we didn’t do a very good job of that, spotted them 10,” Fitzgerald said. “But we responded to that. We started moving the ball. We just sputtered. Credit Notre Dame. They have a darn good football team. We couldn’t give them the things we gave them and expect to win the game.</p><p>“I think we took a step today, from a maturity standpoint, but we did not from an execution standpoint.”</p><p><b>Irish shut down Spartans' run game</b></p><p>Notre Dame has held its last four opponents to fewer than 100 yards rushing. The Fighting Irish limited Michigan State to 44 yards on the ground — none in the second half. The Spartans' Cam Edwards entered the game leading the Big Ten in rushing and was fifth in the nation, averaging 125 yards per game. He finished with 12 carries for 38 yards.</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>Michigan State showed plenty of fight, and there should be optimism in East Lansing that the Spartans can finish with their first winning season since 2021.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Notre Dame: At Purdue next Saturday.</p><p>Michigan State: Hosts Nebraska next Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Aidan Chiles and Joseph Himon lead Northwestern to rout of visiting Colorado
entries.summary: <p>Aidan Chiles passed to Joseph Himon II for three touchdowns and ran in two himself to lead Northwestern to a 41-7 rout of Colorado on Saturday night in Evanston.</p><p>Chiles finished with 241 yards on 17-for-22 passing and upped his season total to seven TDs – four passing and three rushing — in his first two games with the Wildcats (2-0). Chiles, a senior, made 20 starts for Michigan State before joining Northwestern during the offseason.</p><p>“There were some plays that certainly went off-script,” Northwestern coach David Braun said of his quarterback, “but his athleticism and his ability to keep the his eyes downfield, that's really hard to defend.”</p><p>Himon caught an 18-yard pass for his first TD, then a 25-yarder and a 3-yard toss as Northwestern (2-0) pulled away on a rainy evening two days after it announced an extension of Braun’s contract through the 2031 season.</p><p>In addition to 46 receiving yards, Himon, a graduate running back, added 28 on the ground. He has four TDs this season.</p><p>Asked about his on-field connection with Himon, Chiles said “keep it open.”</p><p>“We worked on it all week,” Chiles said. "We knew what we were gonna' get and we came out and executed.</p><p>“There were things that we saw that we knew we could exploit," Chiles added. ”I've talked to the coach, like he's given me the reins, like that's my job. I'm supposed to drive the car to lead the team and that's what I'm here to do."</p><p>Jackson Kleather kicked a pair of field goals in the fourth quarter and hit five extra-point attempts.</p><p>Colorado’s Julian “JuJu” Lewis threw for 168 yards and a touchdown to Joseph Williams on 19 for 29 passing as the Buffaloes (2-1) suffered their first loss after edging Georgia Tech, then routing Championship Subdivision foe Weber State last week.</p><p>Williams finished with 88 receiving yards and JaQuail Smith led the Buffaloes with 91 yards on the ground</p><p>The Buffaloes committed three key turnovers – two fumbles, one interception – in the first half. Two led to quick Northwestern scores.</p><p>The Wildcats led 21-0 at halftime.</p><p>Chiles ran left on a 1-yard keeper with 43 second left in the first quarter to open the scoring. Micah Welch fumbled at the Colorado 44-yard line to let Northwestern start the drive.</p><p>Lewis’ pass up the middle intended for Williams was intercepted by Braden Turner at the Colorado 40 midway through the second. Two plays later, Chiles hit a wide open Himon on the left side with an 18-yard pass to up the lead to 14-0.</p><p>Damian Henderson II was stopped, getting only one yard, on a fourth-and-2 rush attempt at the NU 28 on the Buffaloes next drive.</p><p>Chiles ran the ball in from the Colorado 3 for his second touchdown of the night with 59 seconds left in the half to extend it to 21-0.</p><p>Williams took off alone down the right side for a 50-yard touchdown dash after taking Lewis’ pass at midfield on the fourth play of the second half to complete a quick 66-yard drive for the Buffaloes' first touchdown.</p><p>The Wildcats and Chiles countered to make it 28-7 midway through the third when he found Himon again, this time with a pass up the middle. Chiles hit Himon with a 3-yard toss with 3:15 left in the third to extend it to 35-7.</p><h3><b>Yards don’t matter</b></h3><p>Colorado posted 348 total yards (to Northwestern's 423) and narrowly lead in that stat at the half. Still Northwestern allowed only seven points.</p><p>Braun pointed to a“bending-and-not breaking” element of his defense, and its ability to force and exploit turnovers.</p><p>“Looking at yardage stats is for losers,” he said. “At the end of the day, it does not dictate winning.”</p><p>Braun did say his team has plenty to “clean up,” including tackling better.</p><h3><b>The takeaway</b></h3><p>Colorado: The Buffaloes were hurt by the early turnovers before Lewis was intercepted again the fourth quarter.</p><p>Northwestern: The Chiles-Himon combo was unstoppable, and Northwestern committed only one turnover. Saturday’s contest was the last played at 12,000-seat Martin Stadium, the Wildcats on-campus home since 2024. They’ll open the new 35,000-seat Ryan Field on Friday, Oct. 2 when they host Penn State.</p><h3><b>Up next</b></h3><p>Colorado: Opens its Big 12 schedule next Saturday at Baylor.</p><p>Northwestern: Faces defending national champion Indiana in Bloomington, Indiana next Saturday to open its Big Ten schedule.</p>

entries.title: Daniel Palencia looks like himself again with 2 dominant innings in Cubs' victory
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — Daniel Palenica appears to have recaptured his form just in time.</p><p>Palencia, who had 22 saves and a 2.91 ERA last season, looked the best he has this season, retiring all six batters he faced in the sixth and seventh innings Saturday in the Cubs’ 5-2 victory against the Reds. He struck out three and averaged 99.5 mph on his fastball, hitting 100 four times. Palenica threw 20 pitches, 15 for strikes.</p><p>And it all happened with the Cubs nursing a one-run lead. It wasn’t the same as getting the last three outs, but it was high-leverage nonetheless as the team inched closer to clinching a wild-card berth.</p><p>“Twenty pitches, probably executed 19,” manager Craig Counsell said. “It was a good sign and an important sign.”</p><p>The Cubs haven’t had a regular closer since Jacob Webb lost the job late last month. Perhaps in the final week of the season, Palenica can reclaim the role he had at the beginning of the season and keep it in the postseason, where he had five scoreless outings out of six last year.</p><p>“The bottom line is Danny’s healthy now, and again, just keep getting him out there, and it’ll click,” Counsell said. “He’s a talented pitcher. I felt like a broken record saying, ‘Just keep getting him out there.’ But that’s what you do with talented players. You keep putting them out there, and they’ll figure it out.”</p><p>“He’s more and more time away from being on the IL,” starter Matthew Boyd said of Palencia, who missed time with a strained left oblique and elbow inflammation. “That’s huge. Those reps, you can’t replicate them. Tonight was exactly who he is, and it was awesome to see.”</p><p>Boyd allowed two runs (one earned) in five innings before Palenica entered. Aaron Civale followed with two-thirds of an inning, then Ryan Zeferjahn with one before Ryan Rolison earned his third save by retiring one batter.</p><p>Rolison is among 14 Cubs with a save this season. Perhaps Palencia will be the only one in the postseason.</p><h3>Happ handling platoon</h3><p>One reason the Cubs acquired Tyrone Taylor before the trade deadline was because Ian Happ has struggled badly against left-handed pitching. The switch-hitting Happ has an .826 OPS against righties and a .494 mark against lefties. The right-handed-hitting Taylor has a .906 OPS against lefties.</p><p>That has relegated Happ, a four-time Glove Glove-winning left fielder, to a platoon role. With Reds lefty Nick Lodolo on the mound, Taylor started in left. Happ pinch-hit for him in the eighth when righty Pierce Johnson entered.</p><p>“That’s just the way it is, unfortunately,” Counsell said. “All of us here have performance standards that we got to live up to. It’s not for lack of trying. But on the flip side of that, how Ian’s handled that part of it has been for the betterment of the team.</p><p>“He always has that on his [mind], and it’s important to him. He gets it. It’s not what Ian wants; he wants to be in there every day. But I think he understands right now against left-handed pitching, Tyrone’s the better option.”</p><h3>Steele decision coming</h3><p>Left-hander Justin Steele struck out five in two scorless innings Friday at Triple-A Iowa, his fourth rehab appearance in his recovery from surgery on his left elbow. He didn’t allow a hit and walked one.</p><p>“It was certainly encouraging,” Counsell said. “He flew back to Chicago; we’ll see him on Tuesday. We’ve got some discussions to have there.”</p><p>If the Cubs think Steele, who hasn’t pitched in a big-league game since April 7, 2025, can help in the postseason, they could put him on the taxi squad, allowing him to travel and serve as an emergency replacement.</p><p>“We’ll see what we think going into the last week,” Counsell said. “There’s a lot of things that factor into it.”</p><p>Elsewhere, right-handed reliever Trent Thornton will pitch Sunday for Iowa in his rehab from a sprained left ankle.</p><h3>The opposition view</h3><p>Last year at this time, the Reds were in the middle of sweeping the Cubs in a four-game series on their way to an 8-3 finish that clinched them a wild-card spot on the last day of the season. This season, they’re trying to play spoiler.</p><p>“I’m jealous,” Reds manager Terry Francona said of other teams, including the Cubs, fighting for playoff spots. “[Friday] night, we were looking at the scoreboard, like [bleep] man, that feeling of anxiety, I kind of miss that.”</p>

entries.title: Youth caregivers shouldn't be backstop for systemic failures
entries.summary: <p>A scam text. A forgotten password. An insurance bill written in a language no one seems meant to understand. For millions of Americans, these are the everyday tasks of caring for an aging parent, and increasingly, of parenting the people who once parented us.</p><p>About <a class="Link" href="https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/ppi/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/caregiving-in-us-2025.doi.10.26419-2fppi.00373.001.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>1 in every 4 Americans</u></a> is now a family caregiver — a 45% increase over the last decade. And since most care recipients are adults over 75, we often frame this as a story about aging boomers. But the untold half of that story is the younger people on the other end of those phone calls, hospital visits and late-night emergencies. Young people who are also, at a time when it feels like the world is imploding, trying to figure out how to live their own lives.</p><p>If this feels unfamiliar, let’s consider the data.</p><p>In the U.S., a <a class="Link" href="https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2024/new-study-reveals-millions-of-young-americans-provide-essential-care-to-adults" target="_blank" ><u>recent national study</u></a> estimates about 1.6 million teens ages 15-18 and 2 million young adults ages 19-22 provide care to adults — about 1 in 10 people their age. <a class="Link" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11980010/" target="_blank" ><u>Other research</u></a> suggests that as many as 5.4 million children and adolescents in this country are quietly supporting parents, grandparents, siblings or other relatives who need help because of illness, disability, mental health challenges or substance use.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-710000" name="module-710000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>A recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/05/magazine/child-family-caregivers-aacy.html" target="_blank" ><u>New York Times Magazine investigation</u></a> makes visible what this data can obscure: When formal care systems fall short, the work does not disappear — it often lands on whoever is at home, including children.</p><p>These are not edge cases. This is a generation quietly holding the infrastructure of American family life together.</p><p>And it’s not just physical care. The Census Bureau found that 4.3 million adults <a class="Link" href="https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2023/06/adults-provided-support-to-parents.html" target="_blank" ><u>sent voluntary financial support</u></a> to their parents in 2020, totaling roughly $17.5 billion. That figure is more than the entire federal budget for <a class="Link" href="https://www.nwica.org/blog/weekly-wic-policy-update-179" target="_blank" ><u>WIC</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/1865/text/pl" target="_blank" ><u>Head Start</u></a> that same year. Programs designed to support children, funded at about the same scale as kids quietly supporting parents.</p><p>This reality lands differently depending on where you sit. In cultures where multigenerational households are the norm and elder care is understood as a collective project, young people may still shoulder heavy responsibility, but they are less likely to do it alone and without support. Elsewhere, where adulthood is framed as a solo achievement and families are often scattered across geographies, reverse parenting often plays out in private, over text and FaceTime, without the community infrastructure that would make it sustainable. Distance compounds everything. When the closest family member is a six-hour flight away, every crisis becomes a logistical emergency on top of an emotional one.</p><p>Certainly, the issue is not whether young people should care for their parents. Love, obligation and reciprocity are part of so many family stories, including mine. The question is why we’ve accepted a system that relies on 22-year-olds to backstop the failures of our health, housing and retirement systems.</p><p>There will be another panicked phone call tonight about a bill, a lab result or a fall. On one end will be a parent who deserves real care; on the other, a young person quietly rearranging their life to provide it. In the space between those two realities, love becomes spreadsheets, airport runs, extra shifts and whispered reassurances at sleepless hours. It is beautiful, ordinary, world‑saving work — and it is far too heavy to keep pretending it can be carried alone.</p><p>As former first lady Rosalynn Carter said, “There are only four kinds of people in the world: those who have been caregivers, those who are currently caregivers, those who will be caregivers and those who will need a caregiver.”</p><p>Which are you?</p><p><i>Joshua Lavra is a New York-based artist, principal at Hopelab and a public voices fellow on youth well-being and power with the OpEd Project and Hopelab.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-240000" name="module-240000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Oliver Moore, Nick Lardis could bolster Blackhawks' depth with second-year leaps
entries.summary: <p>After years of lacking star power beyond Connor Bedard, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> hope and expect to have more difference-makers at the top of their lineup this year.</p><p>Summer additions Bowen Byram and Patrick Kane and talented European rookies Anton Frondell and Roman Kantserov all have star potential. The Hawks will need at least two or three of those guys to be exceptional to make their playoff ambitions realistic.</p><p>But the Hawks will also need more depth. The Hurricanes demonstrated the value of that last spring during their Stanley Cup run, which they accomplished without any superstar-caliber linchpins. Hawks coach Jeff Blashill has discussed that repeatedly in recent weeks.</p><p>"Good teams have two lines," Blashill said Friday. "Really good teams have three."</p><p>Within the Hawks' forward group, Nick Lardis and Oliver Moore stand out as second-year NHL players who have the potential to become important secondary contributors in different ways.</p><p>Both opened training camp in significant roles: Lardis on the second-line wing, Moore as the third-line center. Both possess one elite skill — Lardis' shot and Moore's speed — that makes them well-suited to fill a specific niche.</p><p>Both are intelligent players who were intentional about observing and learning as much as possible during their rookie seasons. </p><p>Both improved noticeably as the season progressed as a result, and it stands to reason that both could take major leaps this season after a summer of applying those lessons.</p><p>They're also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/01/10/blackhawks-nick-lardis-settling-nhl-oliver-moore-friendship-shootouts" >close friends</a> who are living together this season.</p><div is actually played. </p><p>He continued doing that during the playoffs — noticing, for example, how the Hurricanes "pressure pucks to create offense" — and during the world championships in May, which he participated in.</p><p>One of his observations: Even though the puck is always moving fast, some star players aren't moving fast all the time, which theoretically gives them more time to process things and anticipate what will happen next.</p><p>This summer, Moore went to work on his own processing and anticipation skills.</p><p>"The biggest thing is just knowing when to make a play," Moore said. "It's hard in summers, but you can work on not forcing it, just holding onto it, making the right play when it's available. At worlds, that was a big thing I tried to focus on: poise with the puck and not just showing it. I like to say, 'The puck is gold.'</p><p>"I talked about not skating myself out of passing lanes and using my brain to navigate a little more. It wasn't as much physical [improvement] this summer; it was more so the mental aspect."</p><p>At center, those skills are especially important, and Moore is happy that Blashill has deployed him into the middle so far. His game "popped," to use his word, once he moved to center last winter.</p><p>Blashill, however, sounds less committed to keeping Moore there long-term, especially once Bedard returns and adds another center to the depth chart.</p><p>"I'm not convinced that he's better at center or wing," Blashill said. "I don't know that answer yet. I don't know that he's played enough. </p><p>"Moore is just going to be a better player this year. It's a year under his belt. It's a year of confidence. It's a year of [experiencing] the ups and downs of pro. He's got an opportunity to be better at both [positions], and we're going to figure it out."</p><p>Lardis, meanwhile, has focused on increasing his speed and explosiveness — as well as his confidence. </p><p>As a rookie, "your confidence isn't fully there 100%," Lardis admitted. But recording seven points (including five goals) in the Hawks' last 13 games — after Blashill finally promoted him above the fourth line — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/04/blackhawks-nick-lardis-confidence-surging-score-in-nhl-connor-hellebuyck" >proved to him</a> that he belonged.</p><p>That was further reinforced by a weeklong trip to Vancouver this summer. It unfortunately came after Bedard's injury, but Lardis felt good about his results training with and competing against Sharks youngsters Macklin Celebrini, Michael Misa and Sam Dickinson.</p><p>Although it's risky drawing strong conclusions from camp practices, Lardis has nonetheless stood out. Blashill agreed with that, noting Lardis has looked "stronger [and] more confident" while skating alongside two talented teammates.</p><p>"I thought Frondell and Bertuzzi played really well together last year," Blashill said. "Frondell has such efficient, good skill, but he also doesn't over-complicate the game. He plays a fairly direct style, and so does 'Bert.' </p><p>"With Nick, it gives them some added skill on that line, and a guy who has the ability to finish. I see Anton making a lot of plays, and...I want another guy on the other side who can finish some of those plays."</p><p>The Hawks sent a roster largely comprised of AHL players to Minnesota for their preseason opener Saturday, a 3-2 overtime loss. </p><p>Their NHL players, including Moore and Lardis, should get to begin testing themselves against real competition for the first time Monday at home against the Wild.</p>

entries.title: White Sox have reached their moment of truth
entries.summary: <p>He used the word ‘‘dog----’’ perfectly. Here, check.</p><p>‘‘Pretty dog----, to be honest,’’ rookie Sam Antonacci said of his play in left field that ended up being the walk-off, two-run double causing the White Sox to lose the crucial middle game of the series against the Guardians that may remain the signature chance to decide and determine the fate of their season. ‘‘Just have to clean it up. It’s the big leagues. You can’t make those types of routes in that position.’’</p><p>Especially when you are in ‘‘their’’ — not just his — position. A position of fear and panic and everything else that comes when expectation finally meets limitations.</p><p>There are words that were used this week to describe the feeling people have for the Sox that the Sun-Times would not allow me to write. Words that make Antonacci’s description seem elementary-school-classroom teachable. And at the core of all of the language of pain, anger, frustration and pisstivity (shout-out to the late, great comedian Robin Harris) is concern.</p><p>A concern rooted more in fear of what could be than of what currently is, of how this has become the other end of the Sox’ bell-curved season, where symmetry is not the balance in which the desired outcome lies. Because expectations have changed.</p><p>Since September’s arrival, the Sox are seven up and 11 down. As the losses have stacked, the swag, grind, hunger and aura of internal invincibility have eroded. Opening the month with a three-game lead in the wild, wild AL Central, only to find themselves 20 days into the month fluctuating anywhere between a game out or up for the division crown and a first-round playoff bye.</p><p>It’s as if their old selves returned just to haunt them to end the season. Bruce Lee famously said, ‘‘Boards don’t hit back.’’ Well, apparently walls do. Because the Sox have hit one. And, from the looks of things of late (before their series against the Tigers), that wall unmercifully struck back.</p><p>Now FOMO has entered The Rate. A division title and possibly the postseason being the ‘‘out.’’ Grateful to ‘‘possibly’’ win the division or to ‘‘have a chance’’ to be in the postseason are no longer aspirations; they remain theirs to lose. Creating a different kind of panic as both city and team slowly watch them — both division title and a front-running season — torturously slip away.</p><p>In the game for first place — the one the Sox insistently needed to win against the Guardians to keep everything they had done since May from going off the rails — in the ‘‘prove themselves’’ series, they didn’t. Making the recent Cubs series against the Brewers (with all of the similarities of importance and timing) take up unwanted space in the backs of the Sox’ minds as to what not to allow to happen. Yet they did.</p><p>It’s that small variance between needing wins to stay alive and needing wins to stay afloat. No life raft.</p><p>Will Venable, whose job security at this point seems in line with Tyler Marsh’s of the Sky, has to tap into the deeper elements of baseball management to revive the Sox for this final sprint they are about to endure. Waiting for Colson Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Miguel Vargas to rescue and carry them offensively no longer seems like a viable strategy. Waiting for Davis Martin, Luis Castillo or even Hagen Smith out of the pen to step up and anchor the pitching staff seems even less feasible.</p><p>Venable’s overthinking (on the South Side, where he’s more protected, it’s called ‘‘out-managing himself’’) is one point of contention. The fall from early grace at the plate simultaneously of three of his best hitters is another. As posted by Elitedingers Sports Page on Facebook going into the series against the Tigers: Since Aug. 30, ‘‘among the 167 players with 50+ [plate appearances], the three worst hitters by batting average are ALL White Sox: 165. Colson Montgomery; 166. Braden Montgomery; 167. Munetaka Murakami. Three of the bottom three.’’</p><p>Add the psychological impact of losing a division lead going into the final week of a season . . . yeah.</p><p>Baseball at this time of the season, when things both large and small are on the line,<br>often comes down to the smallest of smallest of things that are the difference. Non-stats, non-analytics, non-baseball technique or non-ritual things. It’s when and where belief becomes tangible, visual, operable, unexpendable.</p><p>The way your top hitters step to the plate, the looks on their faces and in their eyes. The body language of your pitchers — starters, relievers and closers — every time they step on the mound, with every pitch. The nuances become the margins. The margins have no room for error. The real in life, as in baseball, is simple: When expectations meet limitations, reality is impossible to avoid. Insecurity becomes both shadow and mirror. Concern becomes infectious and contagious.</p><p>This is the season where the ‘‘O’’ in the Sox’ name finally re-replaced the ‘‘U’’ that had seemed to be the team’s brand identity. No more of the same. New dawn, new day. The sun had returned to the South Side, no longer sons to their own oligarchy.</p><p>The Sox will rise. They did. Earlier. Now can they rise to the occasion?</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Good Neighbor Learns Inclusivity Has Limits
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a single woman in a friendly neighborhood. Every month, I have the neighbors over for dinner and a movie. I like to be inclusive — bring the kids, bring the dogs! One couple recently had their elderly mom move in, and I installed a ramp so she could join us. Babies cry, dogs bark, women breastfeed, but all are welcome. I put sleeping bags on the floor for the kids to sit on while grownups sit on the couches. Cleanup is a bear, but every squished meatball on the floor reminds me how much I love everyone.</p><p>Recently, a new couple moved in, so of course I invited them and their 6-year-old to join us. They warned me that he has severe autism, but I told them everyone is welcome, that he wouldn't be expected to be quiet and that the house is thoroughly kid-proofed. When the family showed up to join us, their child was horrible, even by my nonexistent standards for kiddo behavior. He screamed, threw food, bit, spit and hit the other kids and the dogs for an hour. Finally, everyone started to leave before the movie was over. The boy's parents really did try their best, and I was genuinely sympathetic.</p><p>They apologized the next day and said that if they were welcome in the future, they would alternate one parent staying home with their son while the other joined us. That sounds reasonable, but I don't like it. I can't be inclusive just when it suits me. They have since invited me to their home for dinner, and their son was just as bad there, banishing my thoughts that maybe it was just a strange house he was reacting to. I don't know what to do with all this. I'm looking for a magic wand. Any suggestions? — <i>NEIGHBORLY IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR NEIGHBORLY:</b> You are a caring, lovely person, but there is no magic wand that will make that child's severe autism and behavior problems go away. Because you are determined to entertain the entire family, the practical solution would be to invite them and their son over on another evening when other children and pets won't be at risk of injury. Your movie night will be history if it is disrupted like that again. While I commend you for wanting to befriend the family, I think the parents had the right solution.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm 70 now, and many of my friends and family spend our time together complaining about their various ailments. I, too, have had some problems but do not make them a part of our visits unless I'm asked about them. How can I rethink how to make these times more positive for everyone involved? — <i>POSITIVE IN OREGON</i></p><p><b>DEAR POSITIVE:</b> Sometimes, people of a certain age talk about their health problems because they have become less active and can find little else to talk about. To keep the energy flowing in a more positive direction, help your friends find hobbies and other interests to discuss. Even if they have medical issues, most people can manage quiet activities like board games, card games, a book club or a knitting circle. If all else fails, you can always ask them about their families as a change of subject.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Bulls preview: Matas Buzelis & Caleb Wilson make team forward thinkers
entries.summary: <p>The Klutch Sports family takes care of the Klutch Sports family.</p><p>If that means 7 a.m. workouts with the “Unc,” himself, LeBron James, well, even better.</p><p>This has been some summer for Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson.</p><p>When he wasn’t serving notice of his arrival to the NBA back in Summer League, he’s been spotted at Cubs games cheering on Pete Crow-Armstrong with teammate Matas Buzelis and Bears quarterback Caleb Williams, balling out with Buzelis in a South Side Pro Run, and most recently working out with James and some other players represented by Klutch Sports.</p><p>The King eyeing his heir?</p><p>Bulls fans hope so. For now, however, Wilson will have to remain the prince that was promised.</p><p>And while he headlines the team’s frontcourt, not all eyes will be on him. Buzelis is 21 and coming off a season in which he hit 173 three-pointers and blocked 116 shots. That’s elite company in NBA history where names like Dirk and KD reside.</p><p>Then there’s the “old man” of the group in 27-year-old Nic Claxton. Before his back betrayed him with issues the last few seasons, Claxton recorded 189 blocks in the 2022-23 campaign and followed that up with a 146-block season.</p><p>By all accounts the back is no longer an issue, which means with Wilson, Buzelis and Claxton the skies above the United Center are basically a no-fly zone for the opposition.</p><p>Even better news for new coach Tiago Splitter? His starting frontcourt doesn’t just rim protect on the defensive end of the floor. All three have the athleticism and versatility to switch onto guards and wings, which at least on paper should make the Bulls a much better defensive team than they’ve been the last few years.</p><p>Offensively? That’s the wait and see. Buzelis and Wilson have already been building a chemistry in runs and team scrimmages, but what will it look like when the lights are on and the games count? It’s looked great this summer. Then again, most everything Wilson touched did.</p><p></p><p><b>FORWARD THINKING</b></p><p></p><p><b>The Starters:</b> Baring an injury setback, the starting frontcourt is already jotted down in pencil with Claxton, Buzelis and Wilson. This could be the most exciting frontcourt the Bulls have had since the Joakim Noach, Luol Deng days.</p><p></p><p>Buzelis – Year 3 is always huge for a young player and Buzelis is no different. It feels like he is on the edge of stardom and the addition of Wilson might only propel that.</p><p></p><p>Wilson – Not only does he want to be the Rookie of the Year for the vaunted 2026 draft class, but he’s chasing overall league greatness. Wilson will be must-see TV this season.</p><p></p><p>Claxton – If the back is truly healthy then the Bulls will have an athletic big patrolling the paint that they haven’t had in quite some time.</p><p></p><p><b>The Reserves:</b> It’s been a little while since the Bulls have had frontcourt depth and a presence on the wings, but this group should change that. Splitter is being handed a versatile group that can gives the opposition different looks.</p><p></p><p>Isaac Okoro – There were some ups and down for Okoro on the offensive end but his defense was never questioned. Is he a key reserve to help lock down second teamers or could he be a trade piece? Time will tell.</p><p></p><p>Jalen Smith – The stretch big upped his game last season, shooting 37.3% from three-point range and averaging 10.2 points per game – his second-highest scoring campaign.</p><p></p><p>Zach Collins – The center was re-signed for a reason as the Bulls love his physicality and presence in the paint. As long as he stays healthy, the Collins-Claxton duo can be a solid one-two punch.</p><p></p><p>Patrick Williams – Does the former No. 4 overall pick even crack the rotation? It will be interesting to see, especially if Leonard Miller has a say in it.</p><p></p><p>Miller – Miller’s April last year for the Bulls? How about 16.1 points and 7.9 rebounds per game, while shooting 57.7% from the field. He did everything the Bulls wanted to see from Williams the last few years.</p><p></p><p>Noa Essengue – The second-year forward has a lot to prove to his new coach and front office, already on thin ice with his questionable play in Summer League. His age (19) does give him some grace but he needs a lot of work still.</p>

entries.title: WATCH: Caleb Williams' wild scramble vs. Vikings
entries.summary: <p>The last time <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/20/bears-vikings-inactives-ozzy-trapilo-tackle-ben-johnson-sunday-home-opener-nfl" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> played at Soldier Field, his scramble-and-throw on the final play of regulation against the Rams wowed the NFL world.</p><p>In his return Sunday, Williams rattled off a run that was almost as impressive in the first quarter against the NFC North rival Vikings.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Caleb Williams putting defenders on skates 😳<br><br>📺 FOX <a href="https://t.co/xtQOfuugi4">pic.twitter.com/xtQOfuugi4</a></p>— FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) <a href="https://x.com/NFLonFOX/status/2101723615083339980?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>On third-and-12 from the opposing 38 on the Bears’ first drive, Williams tried to slip out of a collapsing pocket to his left, only to be cut off by the Vikings.</p><p>He turned his back to the line of scrimmage and ran back to his right. He went 19 yards behind the line of scrimmage as he looped back, high stepping as defensive end Dallas Turner dove to try to trip him up. Williams ran all the way back to the right sideline, where he slammed on the brakes as Levi Drake <br>Rodriguez dove to try to tackle him. </p><p>He was eventually pushed out of bounds after a six-yard gain. It was enough to set up Cairo Santos’ 50-yard field goal to tie the game.</p>

entries.title: At least Joe Biden isn't being airbrushed away — yet
entries.summary: <p>In this job, it helps to have stock phrases. That way, you don't have to think up something new and clever every time you answer an email. </p><p>For instance, if a reader writes to me, confused — my lucid, well-reasoned argument is just <i>crazy</i> to them — demanding I hold their hand and explain it to them again, perhaps using a felt board, I barely pause.</p><p>"Sir, I have found you an argument," I reply, quoting Samuel Johnson. "But I am not obliged to find you an understanding."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-430000" name="module-430000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Not many actual Nazis write. But when imitators and admirers share their thoughts, to stretch the term, often in an argot I call the Fascist Plural, "We were amused at your feeble Semitic attempt at..." I often deploy a line that is my own, though well worn from use.</p><p>"You know, the whole Nazi thing didn't work out so well for the Germans."</p><p>It really didn't. What gets overlooked in the glare of their crimes — at least 70 million people killed in World War II — in this toll includes 7 or 8 million German citizens and soldiers. Quite a lot really. Not to mention their country pulverized and divided in half, with the Soviets ushering in a half century of jackboot repression.</p><p>What I'm really saying is, "Look to history." Because history is a guide.</p><p>We see how hatred blows back in the face of the hater. The old adage "hatred is taking poison and expecting someone else to die," is true, and on a national scale, multiplies. Didn't end well for Hitler. Despots, surrounded by yes men, make awful blunders. Mao's Communists remained in power, so got to write their history. But 30 million Chinese died in Mao's incompetence-induced famines.</p><p>They don't teach that in China. Squelching history is what totalitarians do. And budding totalitarians.</p><p>This past week, the U.S. Interior Department announced it will be putting warning signs outside the Smithsonian, advising the displays within are hopelessly biased (every accusation of this administration is a confession) because they include bad stuff, and not the cavalcade of greatness leading up to the apotheosis of national joy, triumph and achievement of Donald Trump, <i>Imperator Supremus Maximae Gloriae.</i></p><p>The whole putting-your-name-on-everything hustle is a play right out of the ancient tyrant playbook. From Ramses II, chiseling his name onto the tombs of the previous pharaohs, including his own father, Seti. To Stalin airbrushing opponents out of historical photos. To our president bent on tearing down the Kennedy Center if his name can't be emblazoned on it, destroying a cultural center that has enriched our nation for over 50 years. Effacing the name of a beloved, martyred president. I remember a time when the shock of that hissy fit, embarrassing in a toddler, would have convulsed the nation. Now it's just another ordinary day. </p><p>Far right nationalism isn't just on the march here. If you need more perspective — and yes, I know the nation is divided between those who figured it out long ago and those who never will — look to Europe. The Germans are at it again. The <i>Alternative für Deutschland,</i> "Alternative for Germany," or AfD, a far right party dusting off the Foreigners = Bad Strategy so popular there in the '30s, shocked that nation earlier this month with a strong election showing in a small state in the former East Germany. They are now a player in German national politics, and it is no mystery the game they want to play.</p><p>"The party’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.blogger.com/blog/post/edit/3972382144120426476/1160597924620426651#" target="_blank" >election platform</a> pledged to push artistic institutions to celebrate prewar German history, break from the influences of multiculturalism and end Germany’s 'guilt complex' about the country’s Nazi past," The New York Times reported Saturday.</p><p>Yeah, can't have schools spilling the beans about the massive ruin that resulted from evil philosophy they're using to try to feel alive today. It's like the Germans brought a tiger cub home and immediately went around the house, throwing away certain books, "Tips for Not Being Mauled by Tigers" and "First Aid for Tiger Owners" and such. Because tigers are so cool.</p><p>The United States is a great country, its history filled with glory — we invented freedom, at least the idea that you could run your own life and not dance to the tune of kings. But it's also filled with a heartbreaking litany of times when we betrayed our best principles.</p><p>Like right now, when our leadership is in the clutches a crybaby who spends his day clutching at glory no rational history nor decent populace would afford him. A blizzard of government snowflakes trying to avoid the ray of the sun that will, please God, someday melt them away.</p>

entries.summary: <p>A South Shore shooting left a 42-year-old man dead and a 15-year-old boy injured Saturday night, Chicago police said.</p><p>The two were in the 1900 block of East 71st Place around 10:30 p.m. when an unknown person pulled a gun and fired at them. entries.title: Chicago under flood advisory, rain cancels Chicago River Swim
entries.summary: <p>The annual Chicago River Swim was canceled early Sunday as heavy rainfall continues to pummel the Chicago area.</p><p>The race organizers said the potential for sewer overflow impacting water quality and the risk for lightning contributed to their decision to cancel. It would have been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/03/12/chicago-river-swim-second-annual-september" target="_blank" >the second Chicago River race</a> in nearly 100 years.</p><p>The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory early Sunday as forecasters expect the rain to continue into Monday. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms started Saturday across the Chicago region.</p><p>Over 550 flights were delayed and 49 were canceled at O'Hare International Airport from Saturday morning to Sunday morning, according to the Chicago Department of Aviation. At Midway International Airport, one flight was canceled and 56 were delayed in that same time period. </p><p>Day two of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/19/riot-fest-day-2-chicago-douglass-park" target="_blank" >Riot Fest was cut short</a> Saturday because of "torrential downpours." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Rain chances will persist through Monday, though threat of heavy rainfall should end by early this afternoon. entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> tackle Ozzy Trapilo, whose lightning-quick recovery from a career-threatening torn patellar tendon led him to practice in full Friday, won't play Sunday against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/19/bears-vikings-what-to-watch-for-sunday-ben-johnson-caleb-williams-has-the-ball-soldier-field" target="_blank" >Vikings</a>.</p><p>The Bears made Trapilo, who was hurt in the Bears' playoff win against the Packers in January, one of their inactive players. It was no surprise — despite Trapilo's practice activity, the team has vowed to handle his rehab with patience. He was a full participant Friday for the first time since he was injured. </p><p>The other inactive Bears on Sunday were quarterback Case Keenum; defensive linemen Jayden Loving and Jamree Kromah and guard Jordan McFadden.</p><p>For the first time since Week 7 of the 2022 season, the Bears didn't have a single player listed as questionable, doubtful or out entering the game.</p><p>The Vikings ruled out quarterback Kyler Murray, cornerback Zemaiah Vaughn, safety Jakobe Thomas, receiver Jauan Jennings, center Nick Samac, tackle Caleb Tiernan and defensive lineman Elijah Williams. Righ tackle Brian O'Neill, who was questionable, will play.</p>

entries.title: Bears' next oppoent: Eagles score TD with 9 seconds left to beat the Titans 24-20
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Jalen Hurts threw a 3-yard touchdown pass to Darius Cooper with 9 seconds left, and the Philadelphia Eagles beat the Tennessee Titans 24-20 on a hot and steamy Sunday.</p><p>The Eagles (2-0) appeared ready to dominate Tennessee. They opened the game by stringing together three straight drives of at least 11 plays.</p><p>The Titans (0-2) sacked Hurts three times and picked him off twice, turning those into 10 points. The second interception set up Joey Slye's 33-yard field goal with 1:56 left, putting Tennessee up 20-17.</p><p>Hurts had 1:56 to drive the Eagles 65 yards for the win. He finished with 264 yards passing and two TDs. DeVonta Smith had 10 catches for 117 yards, Tank Bigsby ran for a TD, and Jake Elliott kicked a 58-yard field goal.</p><p>Cam Ward got the Titans (0-2) to midfield, but his final pass under pressure hit the turf harmlessly as time expired.</p><p>Philadelphia improved to 15-4 in September since 2021 and remained tied with Buffalo for the most wins in the NFL's opening month in that span. The Eagles had plenty of fans in the stands, making it feel more like a home game.</p><p>The temperature reached 98 degrees in the fourth quarter and felt like 106 degrees. It measured at least 150 degrees on the artificial surface at Nissan Stadium, so hot the Titans squirted water on players' cleats on the sideline to cool them off.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">When in Nashville… 😂 <a href="https://t.co/NWepuwjpkP">pic.twitter.com/NWepuwjpkP</a></p>— FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) <a href="https://x.com/NFLonFOX/status/2101736833084428667?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Titans hadn't started a season with back-to-back home games since 2010. It didn't help new coach Robert Saleh as Tennessee lost its first two for a third straight season.</p><p>Ward threw for 183 yards and ran for a pair of 1-yard TDs.</p><p>Three-time Pro Bowl running back Saquon Barkley suffered a stinger in his left arm on the opening play, though he returned to start the third quarter. He finished 9 yards on four carries, his fourth career game held under 10 yards rushing.</p><p>Philadelphia seemed ready to run the Titans off their own field, starting the game with a 15-play drive. But Hooker picked off Hurts' pass to Smith in the end zone and set up Ward's 1-yard TD run for the lead.</p><p>The Eagles led 14-10 at halftime despite holding the ball for nearly 22 minutes. Slye pulled the Titans closer with a 37-yard field goal as the second quarter expired.</p><h3>Injuries</h3><h3></h3><p>Eagles TE Dallas Goedert hurt a knee midway through the second quarter.</p><h3>Up next</h3><h3></h3><p>The Eagles play the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> at Soldier Field on Monday, Sept. 28.</p><p>The Titans visit the New York Giants next Sunday.<br></p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams hurts hamstring on non-contact play in 9-3 loss to Vikings
entries.summary: <p>Quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/20/bears-vikings-caleb-williams-watch-wild-scramble-sunday" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> hurt his right hamstring on a non-contact play midway through the fourth quarter of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' 9-3 loss to the Vikings on Sunday.</p><p>He fell to the ground screaming after rolling to the left on a first-and-goal pass at the Vikings' 6. He slid to the ground for no-gain. He went to the blue medical tent and was eventually taken on a golf cart to the Bears locker room. Williams had a towel over his face but took it off and pumped his fist in the air as he reached the tunnel at the northwest side of Soldier Field.</p><p>The Bears will evaluate Williams again Monday after doing further imaging. Coach Ben Johnson said he was "happy it was nothing with the knee," but admitted that the "hamstring could be damaging as well." He spoke to Williams shortly after the game ended and said the quarterback was in good spirits.</p><p>Williams walked through the locker room carrying his duffel bag, seemed upbeat, said hello to people. He said "all good" as he walked past Tyson Bagent's media scrum and left the locker room.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Bears QB Caleb Williams was helped off the field after going down with an apparent injury in the 4th quarter vs. the Vikings.<br><br>(📺 FOX) <a href="https://t.co/0RgMh8ZimH">pic.twitter.com/0RgMh8ZimH</a></p>— SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) <a href="https://x.com/SportsCenter/status/2101757253866881218?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>When Williams was hurt, a hush fell over a damp Soldier Field, which had watched the Bears struggle to just three points one week they scored 59 points in a win against the Panthers. The mood grew even more somber three plays later, when Cairo Santos' chip shot field goal, which would have tied the game, was blocked by the Vikings' Isaiah Rodgers. </p><p>Down six with a minute to play, Bagent took over at the 35 and completed his first two passes to Luther Burden before spiking the ball at the Vikings' 41 with 38 seconds left. He lofted a pass right to Rome Odunze for 21 yards on the next play. After an eight-yard completion to Burden, Bagent threw incomplete along the left sideline, leaving third-and-two from the 12 with 5 seconds to play. After an incompletion, Bagent took the snap with 1 second left at the 12 yard line — and was sacked by edge rusher Dallas Turner.</p><p>Williams hurt the same hamstring during the Pac-12 championship game while at USC. Before Sunday, Williams had been remarkably durable during his three-year NFL career, never missing a significant snap at any point in his NFL career. Williams was one of the darlings of the NFL offseason, landing a "Madden" cover and visiting sporting events across Chicago as a prominent fan.</p><p>He finished the game 15-for-26 for 138 yards, one interception and a 56.2 passer rating. </p><p>The Bears trailed the Vikings 6-3 at halftime with their only points, a 50-yard Santos field goal, coming after Williams' wild scramble. A D'Andre Swift fumble at the 1-yard line and Santos' blocked kick kept the Bears shut out throughout the second half. The Vikings' Will Reichard made his third field goal of the game with 1:09 to play to go ahead by six. </p><p>The Bears have eight days until their next game, a Monday night matchup against the Eagles at Soldier Field.<br></p>

entries.title: Bears' grades are in. How did they do against the Vikings?
entries.summary: <p>To the highly trained eye, there was something about the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' 9-3 loss to the Vikings in their home opener at Soldier Field that didn't quite resemble their 59-point outburst in a Week 1 win at Carolina.</p><p>Hmm, what could it have been?</p><p>Ah, yes — all-out disaster.</p><p>Let's get to the grades. Warning: They're ugly as sin.</p><p><b>QUARTERBACK — C-MINUS</b></p><p>Caleb Williams went down with a hamstring injury in the red zone in the fourth quarter, a gut punch to the Bears and their fans on a drive that ended up producing no points to pour salt in the wound. Before that, Williams’ best moments were jukes and spin moves on desperate scrambles that didn’t really amount to anything important. It’s hard to dock him too much for the Bears’ nonexistent passing attack considering how little time he had to operate, but he hardly was sharp when he did get a pass off. Tyson Bagent came in and led a promising final drive but, when he needed it, had no magic up his sleeve.</p><p><b>OFFENSIVE LINE — F</b></p><p>A million times, F. From center Garrett Bradbury’s cavalcade of first-half penalties to the unit-wide inability to create running lanes or protect their star QB, the Bears got their tails utterly handed to them up front. What a bitter pill to swallow and a giant step back.</p><p><b>RUNNING BACKS — D</b></p><p>Kyle Monangai ran hard, averaging 4.7 yards per carry, and D’Andre Swift had a beautiful 32-yard catch and run in the fourth quarter that looked like it might set up the Bears for a go-ahead touchdown until everything blew up in their faces. But Swift’s earlier fumble on first-and-goal from the 1 was a devastating mistake — as bad as the offense was, maybe the Bears are 2-0 if Swift hangs on to the ball there — and the running backs had a rough day in the pass-protection department.</p><p><b>WIDEOUTS AND TIGHT ENDS — F</b></p><p>Wait, what pass catchers? Rome Odunze couldn’t squeeze a third-down slant that would’ve moved the chains. Luther Burden didn’t show up until very late. The tight ends were no-shows, other than when it came to some glaring errors. Was there any type of mistake — penalties, missed blocks, a dropped potential touchdown pass — rookie Sam Roush didn’t make?</p><p><b>DEFENSE — B</b></p><p>You hold the other guys to nine points, you deserve an overall tip of the helmet even though the Bears gave up 100-plus on the ground to run-of-the-mill Aaron Jones and didn’t create any turnovers or make any truly big plays on that side of the ball. Lineman James Lynch was stout against the run, for whatever it’s worth. It’s not the “D’s” fault the Bears blew an opportunity to win a division game against far-past-his-prime QB Carson Wentz.</p><p><b>SPECIAL TEAMS — F</b></p><p>Getting a 23-yard field goal try blocked when the Bears absolutely had to have it in the fourth quarter was pathetic. Guess who got beat on the play by Isaiah Rodgers, who crashed around the end to block it? Yep, Roush.</p><p><b>COACHING — D</b></p><p>Ben Johnson’s gutsiest decision was to go for it on fourth-and-one in the red zone in the fourth quarter, the Bears down 6-3, and they converted. On the whole, though, Johnson got his lunch handed to him by Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores.</p>

entries.title: Review: Phoebe Bridgers takes Chicago off-the-grid for a phone-free ‘Lost Weekend’
entries.summary: <p>With a strict no-phones policy, a heap of ethereal indie-folk-rock cuts and a set design that could convince someone they had an encounter of the third kind, singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers took fans off the grid for an emotional stop on her headlining arena tour at the United Center on Saturday.</p><p>Bridgers held court on two stages, one anchored by her nine-piece band, and the other mostly reserved for more stripped-down arrangements. A gulf of adoring fans separated the two raised platforms, as thousands in the arena’s seats watched with full attention — low-lit masses devoid of the white glow of a cellphone screen. All eyes were trained on the 32-year-old singer-songwriter who wore a gray quarter-sleeved dress with sparkling makeup that looked like tears dried in silver. </p><p>Bridgers’ legion surrendered their phones at the UC’s front gates to security, who also quickly sealed smartwatches and other devices in a Yondr pouch connected to a lanyard that some wore around their necks like a dog cone.<b> </b><b> </b>Others excitedly draped the pouch like a cross-body bag as if it were a welcomed part of the tour, which has been shrouded in mystery for fans clamoring for details online. </p><p>“I already feel like crying,” one woman told her friends through a big smile, clutching her pouch on the way toward a long merch line. </p><p>It wasn’t clear on Saturday where one could go if they needed to unlock their pouch. Security told a Sun-Times reporter that they’d unlock the phone in an emergency, “but for text sending, go to the atrium.” </p><p>While Bridgers is not the first entertainer to use Yondr pouches, her choice is notable because of her Gen Z-Millennial fan base. That much was clear during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/9/10/22667748/pitchfork-music-festival-union-park-day-one-band-reviews-phoebe-bridgers-dehd" target="_blank" >Bridgers’ 2021 Pitchfork Fest performance in Union Park</a>, where hundreds of phones went up to film the chorus of “Kyoto,” one of her most popular songs.</p><p>“Kyoto” was still one of Saturday night’s biggest sing-alongs, but it was striking to scan the crowd and see seemingly everyone hands-free, lifting their voices and moving to the music. Security armed with binoculars and radios also scanned, ready to toss any scofflaws.</p><p> Additionally, the mass chorus was a clear testament to Bridgers’ sky-rocketing fame in the last 10 years, with career highs that include the release of three solo albums and Grammy Award-winning collaborations with R&B songstress SZA — and fellow folk-rockers Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus via their side project boygenius. </p><p>Saturday marked the second of Bridgers’ two-night stint at the UC for her “Lost Tour,” in support of her first solo full-length album in six years. “Lost Weekend,” released Aug. 14, has the type of raw lyricism and sweeping arrangements that have endeared Bridgers to an ardent fan base — and builds on those themes of love and loss to reach acceptance, aided by a progressive blend of synth beds and folk rock instrumentation.</p><p>The show began with the low chromatic tones of Bridgers’ voice through a vocoder on “The Outside,” sounding like a millennial Laurie Anderson, as the crowd hushed to near silence and faced a mysterious dome covering the main stage. The song transported fans to her father’s funeral in 2023, when she sang: “One more time for old time’s sake, I’ll watch him get carried away,” employing a devastating dark humor to process loss and a complicated relationship.</p><p>She continued that exercise over the course of her stellar, hour-and-forty-five-minute set on Saturday, a show that successfully took the quietness of her guitar-driven songs to flashy arena-headlining heights without sacrificing the intimacy she has become known for.</p><p><b> </b>Though the United Center might be one of the worst-sounding venues in Chicago, a place where a snare might hit you three beats later, Bridgers and her band overcame the sonic obstacle to deliver fully realized interpretations from her catalog. That was a credit to key members like Madden Kass on drums and frequent collaborator Melina Duterte, also known as Jay Som, deftly juggling trumpet, acoustic guitar and synths.<b> </b></p><p>The dome covering the main stage would eventually steam and slowly lift, revealing Bridgers and co. once they kicked into “Motion Sickness,” eliciting loud cheers as she guided them through a set list featuring a balance of new songs from “Lost Weekend,” and passionate sing-alongs of her older material.</p><p> Throughout the night, the stage’s dome would at times hover directly above Bridgers and her band, like a spaceship ready to collect, or tilt back to resemble a planetarium with celestial projections. A ball of light hung above the second stage, just past mid-court, like an extraterrestrial tool that would cast multicolor eruptions and shades of a pale blue motif.</p><p>About midway through her set on Saturday, Bridgers took the second stage for a particularly gutting string of songs, including “Funeral” (2017), about depression and grief, and “Graceland Too” (2020), about unending support for a loved one enduring mental health crises. Band members accompanied her with a fiddle, electric upright bass and banjo. When the crowd wasn’t singing along, they were virtually silent, save for a smattering of sniffles. </p><p>“We all crying!” a fan could be heard telling a teary friend. </p><div class="Enhancement" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Matt Grubb/Instagram: @mattgrubb.americas.waffle</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Alone on the second stage, Bridgers elaborated on her decision to ban phones, explaining that she’s had a hard few years, acknowledging that many people share that same experience. For her, she said, processing the death of her dad amid outside attention feels impossible — it’s hard to cry with camera phones trained on you, she said, though she “knows it’s annoying to give up your phone for a couple of hours.” That people were willing to come and do that meant a lot to her, she said to cheers.</p><p>“Shoutout to anyone who has a complex relationship with their parents. I love you,” she said, before going into “Still Standing,” a heart-wrenching song about her father. “I can't imagine you dead, but you are every day — thank you for everything,” she sang to a reverently silent arena that flickered in various places with fans holding lighters.</p><p> She followed with another heartbreaker on “As Above,” her voice rising from its signature whisper to belt: “You won’t have to believe in magic, leave it to me and I’ll make it happen.” Her band pounded away on the main stage, and a glitter-like material fell above her, looking like stardust. She left for a cleared path in the crowd to join her band, still chanting the chorus, her arms outstretched, touching hands reaching for her like some melancholy messiah. </p><p>Spending a largely distraction-free night with Bridgers’ music means a soul-wrenching dive into the depths of the musician’s emotional interior and your own. That made the moment she burst onto the main stage with “Bobby,” a major-key ode to finding new love, feel all the more hard-won. “This could be the end of wanting,” Bridgers sang, eyes closed.</p><p><b> </b>One of her final songs of the night, “I Know the End,” from 2020’s “Punisher,” concluded with her leading the room in a guttural scream — a release after a night of hard emotional labor. </p><p>Back on the second stage with “Scott Street” from her 2017 debut “Stranger in the Alps,” she capped the night with the house lights up for one last sing-along, bodies swaying. It was the kind of thing many might reach for their phones to capture, but on Saturday, it was a moment, then a memory.</p><p>“Thank you for an incredible two nights, Chicago!” Bridgers said while exiting, as her band played her out and sang: “Never going back again, the way it used to be is not that way it is,” driving home a reality for concertgoers.</p><p>Aside from any merch or dried tears fans headed home with, the last two nights in Chicago are now a memory, and over time, might fade into a lost weekend. </p><h3>Phoebe Bridgers set list for Sept. 19, 2026 show at United Center</h3><p>Motion Sickness<br>The Governor's Waltz<br>Lost Boys<br>DVD Menu (instrumental)<br>Garden Song<br>Moon Song<br>Liberty Tree<br>Panorama (instrumental)<br>Lost Weekend<br>Funeral<br>Graceland Too<br>Haunted<br>Still Standing<br>As Above<br>Bobby<br>Sidelines<br>Georgia<br>I Can't Wait<br>On Video<br>Kyoto<br>I Know the End<br>Lost Weekend (Reprise)<br>Scott Street<br>Never Going Back!</p>

entries.title: Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman leaves game after being hit in face by foul ball
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> third baseman Alex Bregman left the game Sunday against the Reds after being hit in the face by a foul ball off Michael Busch's bat while standing near the on-deck circle. </p><p>Bregman wasn't in the circle; he was standing on the grass, not that far from the plate. The left-handed-hitting Busch checked his swing on a pitch from Reds righty Luis Mey, and the ball bounced before striking Bregman. He appeared to get hit just below his left eye, and blood dripped from his face. </p><p>Matt Shaw pinch-hit for Bregman, who had an RBI single in the first inning. He also walked and scored in the Cubs' four-run third. </p>
